apps.name: OpenMasjid Companion
apps.tagline: Prayer times and giving, on every musalli's phone
apps.author: OpenMasjid-Solutions
apps.description:
**OpenMasjid Companion** puts your masjid in your congregation's pocket. Put a QR
code on the noticeboard; anyone who scans it gets your prayer timetable on their
phone — and can add it to their home screen like an app, with no app store and
nothing to sign up for.

- **Your timetable, not a calculated one** — today, this week and this month come
  straight from **OpenMasjid Display**, so the times on a phone are the same times
  that are on the wall, including any Iqamah change you have scheduled.
- **A countdown to the next Iqamah**, with Jumu'ah, the Hijri date, and a page
  that looks like the time of day — dark before Fajr, light by mid-morning, dark
  again after Maghrib. Calm, and easy to read one-handed at Fajr.
- **Works with no signal** — the last timetable it fetched stays on the phone, and
  it says plainly when it was last updated rather than guessing.
- **Optional prayer reminders** — a musalli can choose which prayers to be
  notified about, at the Adhan or a few minutes before the Iqamah. It is their
  phone's choice, per device, and you never see who subscribed — only how many.
  They come from your own box, with no outside notification service involved.
- **Announcements** — type a notice, for a funeral, a closure or a changed Iqamah,
  and it reaches every phone that has not turned notices off, with your masjid's
  name on it. You confirm first, because it cannot be taken back. One can also be
  set to send itself: once on a date, every day, or on chosen days at a chosen
  time, on your masjid's own clock.
- **A Qibla compass**, from the phone's own location — which never leaves the
  phone and is never stored.
- **Your appeals, in the app** — paste the share link of any appeal from
  **OpenMasjid Donations** and it appears as a tile with its progress. Tapping
  **Donate** opens your Donations page to give; this app never handles money.
- **Your contact details** at the top of Settings — phone, email, address, website
  and links to WhatsApp, Instagram, Facebook, X, YouTube or Telegram. Fill in as
  much or as little as you like; anything blank is simply not shown.
- **A QR code and a printable poster.** The code points at a page that walks people
  through installing it, and that page knows which phone and browser is reading it
  — including what to do when *Add to Home Screen* is missing from an iPhone's
  Share sheet. The admin panel then tells you how many phones opened the app and
  how many kept it on their home screen, which is how you know the poster worked.
  It counts phones, never people, and forgets after 90 days.

**Before it can reach a phone, turn on Remote access.** This app is only useful
over the internet — a QR code pointing at an address inside your building works
for nobody outside it. Install it, open it, and it walks you through switching
Remote access on in OpenMasjidOS and sharing this app; until then it says so
plainly instead of showing a link that cannot work.

**Nothing to fill in at install.** Open it and set it up inside: pick your
timetable, paste your appeals, name the app and choose its icon, then print the
poster.

alerts.label: Prayer times source unavailable
alerts.description: The Companion app hasn't been able to read the timetable from OpenMasjid Display for several hours, so phones are showing the last times it managed to fetch. Usually this means Display was updated, st

alerts.label: Prayer notifications failing
alerts.description: Prayer reminders are being rejected in bulk by the phones' push services — not one dead handset, but most of them. Nobody is getting reminders until it is looked at.

alerts.label: Test alert
alerts.description: A test you trigger from the app (Settings → "Send me a test alert") to confirm OpenMasjidOS is reaching you by email or webhook.

apps.compose:
# SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-only
# Copyright (C) 2026 OpenMasjid-Solutions

# OpenMasjid Companion — one container that runs everything: the musalli app, the
# admin panel, the API, the push scheduler and the SQLite store. One image to
# install, one to update. Least-privilege: no privileged mode, no host networking,
# no devices, no Docker socket.
#
# Nothing to configure at install time. The platform will ask one question — whether
# to share this app over the internet — because manifest.yaml sets `tunnel: true`,
# and that is the one answer this app genuinely needs. Everything else is chosen
# inside the app and saved to /data.
services:
  app:
    # ── MAIN BRANCH: the stable channel ──────────────────────────────────────
    # The release version, pinned to the manifest-list @sha256 digest of the image CI
    # published for it. The digest is what protects an existing install: every push to
    # main republishes :<version> and :latest, so a version tag on its own is NOT
    # immutable — the digest is the only thing that is.
    #
    # It must be the MANIFEST-LIST digest, never a per-architecture one: a per-arch
    # digest pins amd64 and breaks every Raspberry Pi in the catalog.
    #
    # The order that produces this line is publish -> pin -> tag (CLAUDE.md §0). It is
    # written in its own commit, after main has published, from a digest read out of
    # the registry for THIS version — never carried over from the previous release and
    # never guessed. `verify-release-tag.yml` re-checks it against GHCR on every v* tag.
    #
    # On `dev` this line is the exact prerelease tag with no digest. Never carry that
    # form into main.
    image: ghcr.io/openmasjid-solutions/openmasjidcompanion:0.2.0@sha256:07d0b2b87a73f60d0e5c84edca34b80284246531f2feb19a94808f4123d50036
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      PORT: "8080"
      DATA_DIR: /data
      # OpenMasjidOS Fabric: the platform writes these into the app's .env and runs
      # compose with --env-file, which only feeds ${VAR} SUBSTITUTION — so they must
      # be referenced here to actually reach the container. Without these four lines
      # single sign-on, the public-URL lookup and the timetable broker call all
      # silently no-op, and nothing anywhere says why. (This is the exact trap that
      # left OpenMasjid Display's SSO dead for several releases.) Empty defaults keep
      # a standalone `docker compose up` quiet.
      OPENMASJID_BASE_URL: ${OPENMASJID_BASE_URL:-}
      OPENMASJID_APP_ID: ${OPENMASJID_APP_ID:-}
      OPENMASJID_APP_SECRET: ${OPENMASJID_APP_SECRET:-}
      # Injected empty when the admin has not shared this app over the tunnel. The
      # live source of truth is GET /api/fabric/site; this is its convenience mirror,
      # and the app treats an empty value as "not exposed yet" rather than a failure.
      OPENMASJID_PUBLIC_URL: ${OPENMASJID_PUBLIC_URL:-}
    ports:
      # host:container. OpenMasjidOS offers "Open" on the lowest published port and
      # picks a different free host port automatically if 7880 is already taken — so
      # nothing in the app may ever depend on this number.
      - "7880:8080"
    volumes:
      - data:/data
    # ── Least-privilege, from day one ────────────────────────────────────────
    # Runs as an unprivileged user with a READ-ONLY root filesystem. The sibling apps
    # both record not having this as a known gap; a new app has no upgrade path to
    # protect, so it starts with it rather than inheriting the gap.
    #
    # The two things this needs in order to work, both handled in the Dockerfile:
    #   * /data is created in the image owned by 1000:1000, so Docker gives a FRESH
    #     named volume that same ownership and the app can write its database.
    #   * nothing is written anywhere else. /tmp is the tmpfs below; the app writes to
    #     /data and nowhere else on disk.
    user: "1000:1000"
    read_only: true
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp

volumes:
  data:

apps.name: OpenMasjid Display
apps.tagline: Run prayer timetables, cameras and HDMI on every screen in your masjid — over your network
apps.author: OpenMasjid-Solutions
apps.description:
**OpenMasjid Display** turns one small computer into the control room for every
screen in your masjid. Each TV gets its own network video link (RTSP) that you
point a cheap "RTSP decoder" box at once — then you decide, from your phone or a
computer, what each screen shows:

- **Prayer timetables** — beautiful, full-screen prayer clocks calculated on the
  device (no internet needed). Make as many as you like, each with its own colours
  to match the room it hangs in. Shows a large live clock, the Hijri and Gregorian
  dates, every prayer's Adhan **and** Iqamah time, Jumu'ah, and a gentle countdown
  to the next prayer with the current prayer highlighted.
- **Cameras** — bring in any security/IP camera or an imam camera and put it on a
  screen with one tap (great for overflow rooms and the women's section).
- **HDMI sources** — plug a laptop or a recording into an HDMI-to-network encoder
  and send it to the screens you choose.

Set it once and forget it: a weekly **schedule** can switch a screen to a camera
for Jumu'ah, then back to the timetable afterwards — automatically. Volunteers can
always take over instantly from the simple mobile page.

It's designed to be light enough for a Raspberry Pi, a mini-PC, or a Proxmox
container, and the whole control panel matches the calm OpenMasjidOS look in both
light and dark.

**Nothing to fill in here — just install.** When it's running, click **Open** —
it signs you in with your OpenMasjidOS login and matches your dashboard's light/dark
look and wallpaper. Then set everything up inside: your masjid details, your screens,
cameras and schedules. Each screen shows you the exact link to paste into its decoder —
no network address to look up.

commands.label: Add a scheduled Iqamah change
commands.description: Set new Iqamah times from a date. Send exit at any point to stop.

apps.compose:
# SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-only
# Copyright (C) 2026 OpenMasjid-Solutions
# OpenMasjid Display — one container that runs everything:
#   • the control panel (web UI + API),
#   • the timetable video renderer, and
#   • the RTSP server (MediaMTX) every screen's decoder connects to.
# Bundling them keeps it simple: one image to install, one to update. It stays
# least-privilege: no privileged mode, host networking, devices or sockets.
#
# Nothing to configure at install time: install it, open the control panel,
# create your password, and set everything up inside the app (saved to /data).
# Screens find this server automatically from the address you open the panel with.
services:
  app:
    # ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
    # │ DEV BRANCH — this line is the ONE difference between dev and main.      │
    # └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
    # It must name the EXACT version in manifest.yaml (X.Y.Z-dev.N), which CI publishes
    # as an immutable tag. Bump both together, every dev build.
    #
    # It used to be the moving `:dev` tag, and that is precisely why development-channel
    # updates never worked: the platform detects an update by comparing the catalog's
    # version against the installed one, so republishing new content under an unchanged
    # version and an unchanged image reference is invisible to it — nothing to notify,
    # nothing to update to. `:dev` is still published as a convenience alias, but the
    # catalog pins the versioned tag, so that is what belongs here.
    #
    # ON MERGE TO MAIN this MUST become a pinned release reference:
    #     image: ghcr.io/…/openmasjiddisplay:<X.Y.Z>@sha256:<digest>
    # because main is what every masjid installs. The `channel` job in
    # .github/workflows/checks.yml fails the build if the version format or ANY image
    # line is wrong for the branch it is on, in either direction. See CLAUDE.md →
    # "Branching policy".
    image: ghcr.io/openmasjid-solutions/openmasjiddisplay:0.70.0@sha256:0cd6f28b7cef15b66a72f06ff3e84eae020d7161cd0f7a05c43d9e501c90122a
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      PORT: "8080"
      VOLUNTEER_PORT: "8081"
      VOLUNTEER_PUBLIC_PORT: "7861"
      DATA_DIR: /data
      # OpenMasjidOS Fabric: the platform writes these into the app's .env and runs
      # compose with --env-file, which only feeds ${VAR} SUBSTITUTION — so we must
      # reference them here for them to actually reach the container (appearance/SSO +
      # notifications). Empty defaults keep a standalone `docker compose up` quiet.
      OPENMASJID_BASE_URL: ${OPENMASJID_BASE_URL:-}
      OPENMASJID_APP_ID: ${OPENMASJID_APP_ID:-}
      OPENMASJID_APP_SECRET: ${OPENMASJID_APP_SECRET:-}
      # Video encoder: unset/x264 (default, always works) | qsv | auto.
      # See the block below before setting this to qsv — it needs a device the App Store
      # install cannot be given. Unset here so it can be supplied via .env / the environment.
      VIDEO_ENCODER: ${VIDEO_ENCODER:-}
    # ── Intel Quick Sync (hardware H.264) — OFF, and it must stay off in THIS file ───────
    #
    # QSV needs the GPU inside the container, i.e.:
    #
    #     devices:
    #       - /dev/dri:/dev/dri
    #
    # That line CANNOT be added here. OpenMasjidOS's compose risk-check treats any `devices:`
    # entry as BLOCKING (packages/core/src/apps/compose-validate.ts — dangers are merged into
    # the refusals that stop an install), so adding it would not degrade the app for masjids
    # without an Intel GPU: it would make the app refuse to install for every masjid, with or
    # without one.
    #
    # A STANDALONE `docker compose up` is a different situation — there is no risk-check, and
    # the operator owns the box. To turn it on there: uncomment the devices block above, set
    # VIDEO_ENCODER=qsv, and check the log says "using Intel Quick Sync". If the encoder or
    # the render node is missing the app says so and stays on libx264 — screens keep working
    # either way, which is the point of falling back rather than failing.
    #
    # For an App Store install this stays unavailable until the platform grows a device
    # allowlist. libx264 is the default and is comfortably fast enough for the timetable
    # stream; QSV is for a box re-encoding several cameras at once.
    ports:
      # host:container. OpenMasjidOS offers "Open" on the LOWEST published port,
      # so the control panel (7860) must stay below the RTSP port (8554). The
      # platform picks a different free host port automatically if one is taken.
      - "7860:8080"
      # The simple mobile volunteer page (off by default; turn it on in Settings).
      - "7861:8081"
      # RTSP video — each screen's decoder connects here (TCP).
      - "8554:8554"
    volumes:
      - data:/data

volumes:
  data:

apps.name: OpenMasjid Donations
apps.tagline: Take card donations on your masjid's network with Stripe
apps.author: OpenMasjid-Solutions
apps.description:
**OpenMasjid Donations** gives your masjid a beautiful, self-hosted donation
website powered by **Stripe**. Put it on a screen by the door with a QR code, or
open it on any phone — a supporter picks a cause, chooses a preset or their own
amount (one-time or monthly), and pays securely by card.

- **Appeals you control** — create as many as you like (General Fund, Zakat,
  Building Fund, Ramadan Appeal…), each with its own wording, images, preset
  amounts and an optional goal.
- **Preset *and* custom amounts** — clear suggested buttons plus a "choose your
  own" field, one-time or monthly.
- **Card payments, on your own page** — powered by Stripe's secure card field.
  Your masjid's card details and keys stay on your device; supporters' card
  numbers go straight to Stripe and never touch this app.
- **A simple admin panel** — manage appeals, see your donations and totals,
  export a spreadsheet, and set your theme to match the rest of OpenMasjidOS.

**Nothing to fill in here — just install.** When it's running, click **Open** —
it signs you in with your OpenMasjidOS login and matches your dashboard's
light/dark look and wallpaper. Then add your Stripe keys and your first appeal
inside the app. It runs happily on a Raspberry Pi or mini-PC, on your masjid's
own network.

alerts.description: A test you trigger from the app (Settings → Email receipt → "Send me a test") to confirm OpenMasjidOS is reaching you by email/webhook.

apps.compose:
# SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-only
# Copyright (C) 2026 OpenMasjid-Solutions

# OpenMasjid Donations — one container that runs everything: the donation site,
# the admin panel, the API, and the SQLite data store. One image to install, one
# to update. It stays least-privilege: no privileged mode, no host networking, no
# devices, no Docker socket.
#
# Nothing to configure at install time: install it, open it, and it takes you
# straight to setup — sign in, then add your Stripe keys and your first appeal
# inside the app (saved to /data).
services:
  app:
    # ── MAIN BRANCH: the stable channel ──────────────────────────────────────
    # Tag for humans + @sha256 digest for integrity (the digest is the real pin — a
    # moved tag can't repoint it to a different image). Bump both on every release.
    #
    # On `dev` this line names that build's exact `X.Y.Z-dev.N` tag, with no digest. That
    # is correct there and wrong here: a merge from dev will try to bring it across, and
    # carrying it into main would point every stable install at a development build. Git
    # conflicts on this line every release — that conflict is a feature, so resolve it by
    # keeping the pinned form below (CLAUDE.md → Branching policy, rule 6).
    #
    # This is the commit the vX.Y.Z tag names — it carries the digest, so anyone pinning the
    # tag gets exactly this image (CLAUDE.md §16.1). The digest is the multi-arch INDEX digest,
    # which is what covers both amd64 and arm64; a per-platform one would break the Pi or the
    # mini-PC depending on which was picked.
    image: ghcr.io/openmasjid-solutions/openmasjiddonations:0.44.0@sha256:e9031387f26fce38e742efbc75df91921ba9495c5a03346ad18e7666ed2c7f8c
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      PORT: "8080"
      DATA_DIR: /data
      # OpenMasjidOS Fabric: the platform writes these into the app's .env and runs
      # compose with --env-file, which only feeds ${VAR} SUBSTITUTION — so they must
      # be referenced here to actually reach the container (appearance/SSO +
      # notifications). Empty defaults keep a standalone `docker compose up` quiet.
      OPENMASJID_BASE_URL: ${OPENMASJID_BASE_URL:-}
      OPENMASJID_APP_ID: ${OPENMASJID_APP_ID:-}
      OPENMASJID_APP_SECRET: ${OPENMASJID_APP_SECRET:-}
      # First-run SEEDS, not install settings — `manifest.yaml` declares no `settings:`
      # block, so the platform never asks for these and never writes them. They are kept
      # for an operator running this container by hand, and are read once at first run;
      # anything saved in the admin panel afterwards wins. The secret key is read
      # server-side only and never sent to the browser.
      STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY: ${STRIPE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY:-}
      STRIPE_SECRET_KEY: ${STRIPE_SECRET_KEY:-}
      STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET: ${STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET:-}
      CURRENCY: ${CURRENCY:-}
      # Fabric Stripe (manifest `stripe: true`): which named OpenMasjidOS payment
      # account this app uses. Blank = the only/first account. The keys themselves are
      # fetched server-to-server from the platform vault (never set here, never stored).
      STRIPE_ACCOUNT: ${STRIPE_ACCOUNT:-}
    ports:
      # host:container. OpenMasjidOS offers "Open" on the lowest published port and
      # picks a different free host port automatically if 7870 is already taken.
      - "7870:8080"
    volumes:
      - data:/data
    # Least-privilege hardening that is safe alongside the named data volume. (Full
    # non-root + read-only rootfs needs an entrypoint to chown the volume and is
    # planned once validated in CI; the container otherwise mirrors Display.)
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp

volumes:
  data:

apps.name: OpenMasjid Kiosk
apps.tagline: Tap-to-donate kiosk for a wall-mounted tablet with a Stripe card reader
apps.author: OpenMasjid-Solutions
apps.description:
Turn an Android tablet and a **Stripe Reader M2** into a beautiful tap-to-donate
station for your masjid. Six one-tap amounts, custom amounts, monthly giving and
email receipts — all managed from a simple admin page on your OpenMasjidOS.

- **Set it up from a web page** — install here, open the admin panel, and browse
  to the setup page on your tablet to download the kiosk app and pair it with a 6-digit code.
- **Reader over Bluetooth or USB** — the Stripe Reader M2 takes the card; card
  numbers go straight to Stripe and never touch this app or the tablet.
- **One-time or monthly** — six preset amounts plus a custom amount, with an
  optional name & email for a receipt.
- **Locked-down kiosk** — the tablet runs as a full-screen giving station and can
  only be exited with a PIN you set in the admin panel.

**Nothing to fill in here — just install.** When it's running, press **Open** — it
signs you in with your OpenMasjidOS login and matches your dashboard's look. Then
choose your Stripe account, design your giving screen, and pair a tablet. It runs
happily on a Raspberry Pi or mini-PC, on your masjid's own network.

alerts.label: Card reader offline
alerts.description: The tap-to-pay reader stopped responding — donations can't be taken until it's back.

alerts.label: A payment couldn't be started
alerts.description: Stripe rejected a payment setup (bad or expired keys, or Stripe is down).

alerts.label: A monthly donation couldn't be set up
alerts.description: A donor asked to give monthly and was charged once, but the standing order could not be created — so nothing will be collected again and they may need telling.

alerts.label: A donor stopped their monthly donation
alerts.description: A donor ended their own standing order using the link in their confirmation email — says who, how much, and which fund.

alerts.label: A donation was refunded
alerts.description: An admin gave a donation back from the Donations screen — says how much, to whom, whether the donor was emailed, and whether a monthly plan is still running.

alerts.label: Test message
alerts.description: A test you trigger from the app to confirm OpenMasjidOS is reaching you.

apps.compose:
# SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-only
# Copyright (C) 2026 OpenMasjid-Solutions

# OpenMasjid Kiosk — one container that runs everything: the admin panel + setup page
# (/new), the API, the SQLite data store, and the bundled Android APK it serves. One
# image to install, one to update. It stays least-privilege: no privileged mode, no
# host networking, no devices, no Docker socket.
#
# Nothing to configure at install time: install it, press Open, and it takes you to the
# admin panel — sign in, choose your Stripe account, design your giving screen, and pair
# a tablet from Devices. All state is saved to /data.
services:
  app:
    # ── MAIN BRANCH: the stable channel ──────────────────────────────────────
    # Tag for humans + @sha256 digest for integrity. The tag MUST match `version:` in manifest.yaml
    # exactly, and the digest is what a masjid actually pulls — so this line is the real integrity
    # pin, and both halves move together on every release.
    #
    # The release order is: merge to main -> CI builds and publishes -> copy the digest it prints
    # ("What was published") back into this line -> tag vX.Y.Z on THAT commit. A push to main is
    # allowed to be unpinned for exactly that one commit, because the digest cannot be known before
    # the image exists; CI warns rather than fails there, and fails hard on a v* tag that is not
    # digest-pinned.
    #
    # NEVER let the dev branch's line survive a merge to main. `dev` carries a bare
    # :X.Y.Z-dev.N tag, and leaving that here would point every stable install at a development
    # build. CI's "Check the compose image matches the channel" step fails the build in both
    # directions — a prerelease version or image reaching stable, or a digest pin stranding dev —
    # but check it by eye too, because a merge is exactly when someone is in a hurry.
    image: ghcr.io/openmasjid-solutions/openmasjidkiosk:0.11.0@sha256:161bc8126a12e70ebd159ed1b7d847c1dc0f44686b8165c75a68526a53097464
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      PORT: "8080"
      DATA_DIR: /data
      # We are always served over HTTPS by the platform (manifest `https: true`), so the
      # session cookie must be marked Secure or the browser may drop it.
      COOKIE_SECURE: "1"
      # OpenMasjidOS Fabric: the platform writes these into the app's .env and runs
      # compose with --env-file, which only feeds ${VAR} SUBSTITUTION — so they must be
      # referenced here to actually reach the container (SSO + Stripe + notifications).
      # Empty defaults keep a standalone `docker compose up` quiet.
      OPENMASJID_BASE_URL: ${OPENMASJID_BASE_URL:-}
      OPENMASJID_APP_ID: ${OPENMASJID_APP_ID:-}
      OPENMASJID_APP_SECRET: ${OPENMASJID_APP_SECRET:-}
      # Our public URL for REMOTE kiosk adoption (manifest `domain: true` + `tunnel: true`). Empty
      # unless the admin turns on Remote access and exposes us. The live source of truth is
      # GET /api/fabric/site; this is the documented convenience mirror.
      OPENMASJID_PUBLIC_URL: ${OPENMASJID_PUBLIC_URL:-}
    ports:
      # host:container. OpenMasjidOS offers "Open" on the lowest published port and picks
      # a different free host port automatically if 7878 is already taken.
      - "7878:8080"
    volumes:
      - data:/data
    # Least-privilege hardening (safe alongside the named data volume) — mirrors the
    # OpenMasjid Donations posture. Drop all Linux capabilities, forbid privilege
    # escalation, and give /tmp its own ephemeral tmpfs.
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp

volumes:
  data:

apps.name: OpenMasjid Students
apps.tagline: Tuition & fees for your madrasa — pay online, at the kiosk, or on the donation site
apps.author: OpenMasjid-Solutions
apps.description:
**OpenMasjid Students** is tuition & fee management built for madāris, running on the
masjid's own hardware.

The office adds **students** (each with an auto-generated **Student ID**), assigns **fee
plans** per student, and generates **one invoice per child** each month or term. A
**finance manager** records cash / Zelle / check payments against the child they were
paid for and sees the whole ledger; **parents** get a phone-first portal showing what
each child owes and one combined balance they can **pay by card in the app (Stripe)** —
with **autopay** and saved cards. Printable statements carry each child's Student ID and
a portal-signup QR.

Tuition can also be paid with a **child's Student ID** on the masjid's **OpenMasjid
Donations** site and **OpenMasjid Kiosk**: type the ID, check the name it shows, then pay
for any of your children from that one screen. Those payments flow straight into the same
ledger over the OpenMasjidOS Fabric. Families can **pay ahead** — a term or a year at a
time, even with nothing due — and the credit comes off their next invoice automatically.

Works fully on the masjid network on its own; parent and finance access can also go over
the OpenMasjidOS internet uplink. (Admin stays on the masjid network by design.)

alerts.label: Autopay switched off after repeated failures
alerts.description: A family's card failed three times, so autopay was turned off. They will not be charged again until someone follows up.

alerts.label: Tuition Student ID lookup locked
alerts.description: One student's ID was locked after repeated failed attempts at the kiosk, the donation site, or parent sign-up — possibly someone guessing IDs.

alerts.label: A payment was recovered by reconciliation
alerts.description: A card payment reached Stripe but never reached the ledger directly; the daily reconciliation found and recorded it. Worth a look.

alerts.label: A payment was only partly recorded
alerts.description: A card payment covering several children was recorded for some of them but not all. The difference has to be entered by hand — check the family's record.

alerts.label: Families are past due
alerts.description: One or more households have a tuition bill whose due date has passed. Open the app to see who, and how much.

alerts.label: A payment was refunded
alerts.description: Somebody in the office gave a tuition payment back. Money leaving is worth knowing about even when it is entirely correct.

alerts.label: Test message
alerts.description: A test you trigger from Settings to confirm OpenMasjidOS is reaching you by email or webhook.

commands.label: Tuition numbers
commands.description: What came in this month, what is outstanding, and how many are behind.

apps.compose:
# SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-only
# Copyright (C) 2026 OpenMasjid-Solutions

# OpenMasjid Students — one container that runs everything: the three role UIs
# (admin / finance / parent), the API, the Fabric provider routes, the printable
# statements and sheets, and the SQLite data store. One image to install, one to
# update. Least-privilege: no privileged mode, no host networking, no devices,
# no Docker socket.
#
# (This header described teachers, a public admissions form and a Stripe webhook
# until 0.48.0. None of the three exist: the academics went in v0.35.0 and there
# has never been a webhook — payments are pulled, see CLAUDE.md §13.4.)
#
# Nothing to configure at install time beyond the settings below — install it, open
# it, create the admin account, and set up the rest inside the app (saved to /data).
services:
  app:
    # ── STABLE CHANNEL — this line differs from `dev`, and that is the point ──
    # Tag for humans + @sha256 digest for integrity. The digest is the real pin: a tag can be moved to
    # point at different content, a digest cannot. This is what every masjid installs.
    #
    # On `dev` this same line is an IMMUTABLE prerelease tag (`:X.Y.Z-dev.N`) matching that branch's
    # manifest version, because the development channel needs a distinct version per build for the
    # platform to detect one at all. So a merge from dev lands a prerelease tag here, and re-pinning is a
    # STEP OF the release rather than an afterthought — CLAUDE.md "Branching policy" + §19: set the plain
    # version, merge, let CI build, pin the digest it prints, then tag.
    #
    # Skipping the pin would ship every stable install a dev build's tag. `build-image.yml` refuses to
    # publish a v* tag whose compose is not digest-pinned, or whose version is still a prerelease — but
    # the guard is the backstop, not the plan.
    #
    # Pinned to the multi-arch INDEX digest, not to a per-platform manifest — so a Raspberry Pi and an
    # amd64 box install the same reference and resolve their own architecture from it.
    image: ghcr.io/openmasjid-solutions/openmasjidstudents:0.51.0@sha256:d5df93e54dfb780fb1e631125356d5887aaf2a3b50e1d74c5f77af43c1fc88af
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      PORT: "8080"
      DATA_DIR: /data
      # OpenMasjidOS Fabric: the platform writes these into the app's .env and runs
      # compose with --env-file, which only feeds ${VAR} SUBSTITUTION — so they MUST
      # be referenced here or SSO / notifications / app-to-app / the tunnel silently
      # no-op. Empty defaults keep a standalone `docker compose up` quiet.
      OPENMASJID_BASE_URL: ${OPENMASJID_BASE_URL:-}
      OPENMASJID_APP_ID: ${OPENMASJID_APP_ID:-}
      OPENMASJID_APP_SECRET: ${OPENMASJID_APP_SECRET:-}
      # Public HTTPS URL from the OS Cloudflare tunnel (manifest `tunnel: true`); used
      # for parent + finance access and for the absolute links in invite, reset and QR
      # codes. Empty when not exposed.
      OPENMASJID_PUBLIC_URL: ${OPENMASJID_PUBLIC_URL:-}
      # No install settings: school name, currency, and the OpenMasjidOS Stripe account
      # to charge through are all configured INSIDE the app (first-run + admin settings,
      # saved to /data). Stripe keys are fetched server-to-server (manifest `stripe: true`),
      # never set or stored here.
    ports:
      # host:container. OpenMasjidOS offers "Open" on the lowest published host port
      # and picks a different free host port automatically if 8360 is already taken.
      # Defence in depth: on an internet-exposed host (e.g. a VPS), firewall this port so
      # it's reachable only on the masjid LAN. The app already denies admin to any non-local
      # client (origin policy, §12.4), but keeping the port off the public internet is wise.
      - "8360:8080"
    volumes:
      - data:/data
    # Least-privilege hardening that is safe alongside the named data volume.
    cap_drop:
      - ALL
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp

volumes:
  data:

apps.name: WhatsApp Gateway
apps.tagline: Let the masjid send WhatsApp messages from a number of its own
apps.author: rmyndharis (OpenWA) — packaged for OpenMasjidOS by OpenMasjid-Solutions
apps.description:
This app lets OpenMasjidOS send WhatsApp messages — fee reminders to parents,
alerts to your team — from a WhatsApp number the masjid controls.

It is a **transport**, not something you use day to day. Once it is linked you
can forget it is here: you set WhatsApp up in **OpenMasjidOS → Settings →
WhatsApp**, and the apps that send (the madrasah app first) ask OpenMasjidOS to
send for them. Nothing else in the masjid talks to WhatsApp directly, and no app
ever sees this gateway's key.

That matters because the risk below belongs to the *number*, not to any one app:
OpenMasjidOS therefore keeps a single, paced, one-at-a-time send queue for the
whole masjid, with quiet hours and a warm-up period for a newly linked number.

## ⚠️ Please read before you link a number

**This is an unofficial WhatsApp client.** It signs in the same way WhatsApp Web
does, not through Meta's official business API. WhatsApp does look for automated
use, and **the number you link can be restricted or banned.** No setting here can
make that risk zero.

**Link a dedicated number the masjid can afford to lose — never the masjid's main
line**, and never a personal number. If the number is blocked you cannot appeal
through us; that is between the number's owner and WhatsApp. Keep email or SMS as
the fallback for anything that truly must arrive.

## What it needs from your hardware

The safer of the two engines (`whatsapp-web.js`, the default) works by running a
real headless Chromium browser, which is why WhatsApp finds it harder to
distinguish from a person. That browser costs **roughly 300–500 MB of memory,
continuously, for as long as the number stays linked.**

On a **2 GB Raspberry Pi this is a heavy app** — it will run, but budget for it
before installing, and expect little room left for other apps. If memory is tight
you can switch the engine to `baileys` (about 30–80 MB), but understand the
trade: upstream rates its ban risk as **higher**, because it speaks WhatsApp's
protocol directly and is easier to fingerprint.

## Setting it up

1. Install this app. Invent a long random **gateway key** when asked, and keep it
   somewhere safe — it is applied when the app first starts, so editing it later
   will not replace it. To change it, use this app's own **API keys** screen.
2. Open this app once (the **Open** button) and create a session: **Sessions →
   New**. Name it anything — `masjid` is fine.
3. Press **Start** on that session. This step is easy to miss and nothing works
   without it: a session that has only been created has no connection behind it
   yet, so linking fails and OpenMasjidOS can only report `gateway returned 400`.
4. Press **View** on the session and copy the **Session ID** from the details
   panel — all of it. The session card shows only the first few characters, which
   is not enough. It is a long code like
   `3f2a1b4c-9d2e-4f6a-b8c1-0d5e7a9f2b3c`, not the name you typed.
5. In **OpenMasjidOS → Settings → WhatsApp**, paste the gateway key and that
   Session ID, then link your number with the pairing code it gives you.

Steps 2–4 are a one-time detour into this app's own screen, and we would rather
they weren't: OpenWA has no way to create or start a session from its settings,
and only it can mint the Session ID. Everything after that happens in
OpenMasjidOS, and you should not need to come back here.

## Kept on your network

The gateway is reachable on the masjid's own network only. It is deliberately not
offered over the internet — it holds a live, logged-in WhatsApp session, and that
is not something to publish. Keep the gateway key secret; anyone on your network
who has it can send as your number.

## Credits

OpenWA is free, open-source software by
[rmyndharis](https://github.com/rmyndharis/OpenWA), MIT-licensed. We package it
unmodified and pin it by image digest; the packaging is maintained by
OpenMasjid-Solutions.

settings.label: Gateway key — invent a long random one, letters and numbers only, and paste the same value into OpenMasjidOS → Settings → WhatsApp. Set on first start only.
Engine — whatsapp-web.js is safer for the number but uses 300–500 MB; baileys uses 30–80 MB and carries a higher ban risk
Memory ceiling for this app — 2 GB suits one whatsapp-web.js session; drop to 1 GB only if you chose baileys

apps.compose:
# SPDX-License-Identifier: AGPL-3.0-only
# Copyright (C) 2026 OpenMasjid-Solutions
#
# OpenWA, packaged for OpenMasjidOS.
#
# This is a PACKAGING repo: the software is OpenWA (MIT, rmyndharis/OpenWA) and we
# run its published image unmodified. Upstream's own docker-compose.yml cannot be
# listed in the catalog — it builds from source, mounts the host Docker socket via a
# socket proxy, and attaches to pre-existing external volumes/networks, all of which
# both the catalog build and OpenMasjidOS refuse at install. So this file is a
# minimal, least-privilege single-service stack: one container, one named volume,
# everything else driven from settings the admin fills in once.
#
# WHAT TALKS TO THIS: only OpenMasjidOS. It finds the gateway on
# 127.0.0.1:<published port> and owns the single paced send queue; apps ask the OS
# to send (POST /api/fabric/whatsapp) and never reach this container themselves.
services:
  openwa:
    # Digest-pinned: the tag alone can be moved to different content.
    # ghcr.io/rmyndharis/openwa:0.21.0
    image: ghcr.io/rmyndharis/openwa:0.21.0@sha256:9adaf792729361ff3fc33defcf9418677ab612cbef2fa5cdcad2b84fe827a318
    restart: unless-stopped
    # The web UI and the REST API are the same port. OpenMasjidOS reads the FIRST
    # published port to find the gateway, so this must stay first and stay published.
    # Published on the LAN (not 127.0.0.1) because the admin has to open this UI once
    # to create the session — see the description. NOT internet-exposed: the manifest
    # deliberately does not opt into a tunnel.
    ports:
      - '2785:2785'
    environment:
      - NODE_ENV=production
      - PORT=2785
      - LOG_LEVEL=info

      # WhatsApp privacy ids (@lid) carry no phone number. OpenMasjidOS identifies a
      # command sender by their number, so without this a lid-addressed sender cannot be
      # matched to the authorised list at all. Resolution is a cached, best-effort engine
      # lookup, only for privacy-id senders — normal numbers are untouched.
      # Upstream defaults it OFF and reads the exact string "true"
      # (feature-flags.ts: `env.RESOLVE_LID_TO_PHONE === 'true'`).
      - RESOLVE_LID_TO_PHONE=true

      # ── Auth ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      # Seeds OpenWA's first API key on FIRST BOOT (auth.service.ts:resolveSeedApiKey).
      # The admin types the same value into OpenMasjidOS > Settings > WhatsApp, which
      # sends it as the X-API-Key header. Changing it later does NOT rotate the key —
      # the seed only applies while no keys exist.
      - API_MASTER_KEY=${OPENWA_API_KEY}
      # Never seed the well-known insecure `dev-admin-key`.
      - ALLOW_DEV_API_KEY=false

      # ── Engine ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      # whatsapp-web.js drives a real headless Chromium, which upstream rates as the
      # LOWER ban risk of the two engines — and the higher memory cost (~300-500 MB
      # per session). baileys is ~30-80 MB and easier for WhatsApp to fingerprint.
      # The `:-` fallbacks matter: a blank answer would otherwise reach the container
      # as an empty string, which OpenWA treats as "pinned to nothing".
      - ENGINE_TYPE=${OPENWA_ENGINE:-whatsapp-web.js}
      - PUPPETEER_HEADLESS=true
      - PUPPETEER_ARGS=--no-sandbox,--disable-setuid-sandbox,--disable-dev-shm-usage
      # Re-start an already-linked session after a restart or a host reboot, so the
      # masjid does not have to re-link. (It cannot CREATE a session — see the README.)
      - AUTO_START_SESSIONS=true
      # One masjid, one number. Also the RAM guard: each extra Chromium session is
      # another ~300-500 MB. Upstream's default of 0 means unlimited.
      - MAX_CONCURRENT_SESSIONS=1
      # OpenMasjidOS sends its own typing indicators, scaled to message length, from
      # its queue. Leaving upstream's on would stack a second delay on every send.
      - SIMULATE_TYPING=false
      # Only read by baileys: upstream's default keeps the gateway marked online,
      # which silences push notifications on the linked phone for as long as it runs.
      - BAILEYS_MARK_ONLINE_ON_CONNECT=false

      # ── Storage: SQLite + local files on the named volume ────────────────────
      - DATABASE_TYPE=sqlite
      - DATABASE_NAME=/app/data/openwa.sqlite
      - DATABASE_SYNCHRONIZE=false
      - SESSION_DATA_PATH=/app/data/sessions
      - STORAGE_TYPE=local
      - STORAGE_LOCAL_PATH=/app/data/media
      - REDIS_ENABLED=false
      - CACHE_ENABLED=false

      # ── Dashboard over plain HTTP ───────────────────────────────────────────
      # OpenMasjidOS serves apps over http:// (https: is reserved for Stripe apps).
      # Left at its production default, the dashboard's CSP upgrades its own scripts
      # to https://, the plain-HTTP server cannot answer, and the page renders BLANK
      # WHITE — upstream #611/#731. This is what keeps the setup page usable.
      - CSP_UPGRADE_INSECURE_REQUESTS=false
      - SERVE_DASHBOARD=true

      # ── HTTP rate limits ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
      # This is the API throttle, not the anti-ban send governor. Sized for the real
      # caller: OpenMasjidOS spends ~5 requests per message (presence, typing on/off,
      # the send, plus status polls) and its own ceiling is 12/hour, so ~60 requests
      # an hour — while leaving the admin's dashboard room to breathe during setup.
      - RATE_LIMIT_SHORT_TTL=1000
      - RATE_LIMIT_SHORT_LIMIT=10
      - RATE_LIMIT_MEDIUM_TTL=60000
      - RATE_LIMIT_MEDIUM_LIMIT=60
      - RATE_LIMIT_LONG_TTL=3600000
      - RATE_LIMIT_LONG_LIMIT=600

      # ── Upstream's own send pacer ───────────────────────────────────────────
      # OFF, on purpose. OpenMasjidOS owns the ONE paced queue for the whole masjid
      # (serialised, jittered, warm-up ramp, quiet hours, per-recipient cooldown).
      # Upstream's governor is a second, independent one: when it refuses it returns
      # HTTP 429, which the platform's queue currently reads as a failed send rather
      # than "retry after N seconds", so a message would be dropped, not delayed.
      # Turn this on only if the platform learns to honour retryAfterSeconds.
      - SEND_PACING_ENABLED=false
    volumes:
      # The WhatsApp session lives here. Without it every restart forces a re-link.
      - openwa-data:/app/data
    # A Chromium per session is the memory story; cap it so a runaway cannot take the
    # whole box down with it. Raise if you deliberately run more than one session.
    mem_limit: ${OPENWA_MEM_LIMIT:-2g}
    # Chromium is multi-process and WhatsApp Web is process-heavy; upstream found 512
    # already kills a session mid-spawn. This is a fork-bomb guard, not an allocation.
    pids_limit: 2048
    stop_grace_period: 45s
    healthcheck:
      test:
        [
          'CMD',
          'node',
          '-e',
          "require('http').get('http://localhost:2785/api/health/ready', (r) => process.exit(r.statusCode === 200 ? 0 : 1))",
        ]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 10s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 60s

volumes:
  openwa-data:
